title: Conservation of mass and balanced equations

notes.definition: The law of conservation of mass states that no atoms are lost or made during a chemical reaction, so the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants. This means chemical reactions can be shown by symbol equations that are balanced in terms of the numbers of atoms of each element on both sides.
explanation: In a chemical reaction the atoms in the reactants are rearranged to make new substances. Bonds are broken and new bonds are made, but the atoms themselves are not destroyed and no new atoms appear. Because every atom that was there at the start is still there at the end, the total mass stays the same. This is the law of conservation of mass: the mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants.

A word equation names the reactants and products, for example magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide. A symbol equation uses formulae instead: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. A symbol equation must be balanced. This means there must be the same number of atoms of each element on the left-hand side (reactants) as on the right-hand side (products). A balanced equation is simply the law of conservation of mass written in symbols.

To balance an equation you may only change the large numbers written in front of formulae, called coefficients. You must never change the small subscript numbers inside a formula, because that would change the substance. For example, H₂O is water but H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide. A coefficient multiplies everything in the formula after it: 3H₂O contains 6 hydrogen atoms and 3 oxygen atoms. A subscript after a bracket multiplies everything inside the bracket: Ca(OH)₂ contains 1 calcium, 2 oxygen and 2 hydrogen atoms.

A good method for balancing is: write the correct formulae; count the atoms of each element on each side; balance one element at a time by adding coefficients, usually leaving elements that appear on their own (such as O₂ or H₂) until last; then recount every element to check. For example, in methane burning, CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O, balancing hydrogen gives 2H₂O, then there are 4 oxygen atoms on the right, so 2O₂ is needed: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.

Because mass is conserved, you can use masses to find a missing mass. If 24 g of magnesium reacts completely with 16 g of oxygen, 40 g of magnesium oxide must form. If a reaction happens in a closed container, such as a sealed flask, the reading on a balance does not change. State symbols show the physical state of each substance: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas and (aq) aqueous, meaning dissolved in water.
keyFacts: No atoms are lost or made during a chemical reaction.
Total mass of products = total mass of reactants.
In a balanced equation there is the same number of atoms of each element on both sides.
Only change the coefficients (big numbers in front) when balancing, never the subscripts.
A coefficient multiplies every atom in the formula that follows it.
A subscript after a bracket multiplies every atom inside the bracket.
State symbols: (s) solid, (l) liquid, (g) gas, (aq) dissolved in water.
In a closed system the mass measured on a balance stays the same during a reaction.
Elements such as hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and chlorine exist as diatomic molecules: H₂, O₂, N₂, Cl₂.

keyTerms.definition: No atoms are lost or made in a chemical reaction, so the mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants.
The substances that react together at the start of a chemical reaction, written on the left of an equation.
The new substances made in a chemical reaction, written on the right of an equation.
An equation that uses chemical formulae to show the reactants and products of a reaction.
A symbol equation with the same number of atoms of each element on both sides.
The large number written in front of a formula in an equation; it multiplies all the atoms in that formula.
The small number in a formula showing how many atoms of the element before it (or groups in the bracket before it) there are.
A system where no substances can enter or leave, such as a sealed flask.

equations.name: Conservation of mass
equations.formula: total mass of reactants = total mass of products
equations.units: g (any mass unit, the same on both sides)

workedExamples.title: Finding a missing mass
workedExamples.question: Calcium carbonate decomposes when heated: calcium carbonate → calcium oxide + carbon dioxide. 25.0 g of calcium carbonate is heated until it has all decomposed. 14.0 g of calcium oxide is formed. Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide formed.
steps: Mass is conserved, so mass of reactants = mass of products.
25.0 g = 14.0 g + mass of carbon dioxide.

workedExamples.title: Balancing a simple equation
workedExamples.question: Balance the equation: Na + Cl₂ → NaCl
steps: Count atoms. Left: Na 1, Cl 2. Right: Na 1, Cl 1.
Chlorine is unbalanced. Put 2 in front of NaCl: Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl. Now right: Na 2, Cl 2.
Sodium is now unbalanced. Put 2 in front of Na: 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl.
Recount. Left: Na 2, Cl 2. Right: Na 2, Cl 2. Balanced.

workedExamples.title: Balancing an equation with brackets
workedExamples.question: Balance the equation for the neutralisation of sulfuric acid by sodium hydroxide: H₂SO₄ + NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O
steps: Treat the sulfate group (SO₄) as one unit because it is unchanged: 1 on each side.
Sodium: 1 on the left, 2 on the right, so write 2NaOH.
Now count hydrogen on the left: 2 (from H₂SO₄) + 2 (from 2NaOH) = 4. Hydrogen on the right is 2, so write 2H₂O.
Count oxygen not in sulfate: left 2 (from 2NaOH), right 2 (from 2H₂O). Balanced.
Final check of every element: H 4 = 4, S 1 = 1, O 6 = 6, Na 2 = 2.

workedExamples.title: Using a balanced equation with masses
workedExamples.question: Nitrogen reacts with hydrogen: N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃. 56 g of nitrogen reacts completely and 68 g of ammonia forms. Calculate the mass of hydrogen that reacted.
steps: Mass of reactants = mass of products.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think you can balance an equation by changing the small numbers in a formula, for example changing H₂O to H₂O₂.
misconceptions.right: In fact changing a subscript changes the substance. Only the coefficients in front of formulae can be changed.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think mass is lost when a substance burns or reacts and seems to disappear.
misconceptions.right: In fact no atoms are lost. If the mass seems to fall, a gas product has escaped; the total mass of all products still equals the total mass of all reactants.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the number of molecules must be the same on both sides of a balanced equation.
misconceptions.right: In fact it is the number of atoms of each element that must be equal. In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O there are 3 molecules on the left and 2 on the right.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a coefficient only multiplies the first atom in a formula, so 2H₂O has 4 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom.
misconceptions.right: In fact the coefficient multiplies the whole formula: 2H₂O has 4 hydrogen atoms and 2 oxygen atoms.

realWorld: Chemical engineers use conservation of mass to work out how much raw material is needed to make a tonne of product, such as ammonia for fertilisers.
Car engine designers use balanced equations for fuel combustion to calculate how much air must be mixed with petrol so the fuel burns completely.
Environmental scientists use mass balances to track pollutants, for example working out how much carbon dioxide is released when a known mass of fuel is burned.
examTips: After balancing, always recount every element on both sides and write the counts down; examiners award the mark only for a fully balanced equation.
Learn the diatomic elements (H₂, N₂, O₂, Cl₂, and the other halogens) so you write correct formulae before you start balancing.
When asked to explain conservation of mass, use the word atoms: 'no atoms are lost or made, they are just rearranged'.
In mass calculations, show the working as mass of reactants = mass of products, then substitute and subtract.
If a question asks for state symbols, include one after every formula in the equation.
summary: No atoms are lost or made in a chemical reaction, so mass is conserved.
Mass of products = mass of reactants.
Balanced equations have the same number of atoms of each element on both sides.
Balance by changing coefficients only, never subscripts.
Coefficients multiply the whole formula; subscripts after brackets multiply the bracket.

flashcards.front: State the law of conservation of mass.
flashcards.back: No atoms are lost or made during a chemical reaction, so the mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants.

flashcards.front: What must be equal on both sides of a balanced equation?
flashcards.back: The number of atoms of each element.

flashcards.front: When balancing, which numbers can you change?
flashcards.back: Only the coefficients (large numbers in front of formulae), never the subscripts.

flashcards.front: How many atoms of each element are in 3H₂O?
How many oxygen atoms are in Ca(OH)₂?
12 g of carbon burns in 32 g of oxygen. What mass of carbon dioxide forms?
What happens to the reading on a balance when a reaction takes place in a sealed flask?
flashcards.back: It stays the same, because no substances can enter or leave.

flashcards.front: Name four elements that exist as diatomic molecules.
flashcards.back: Any four of: H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂.

flashcards.front: Why can't you balance H₂ + O₂ → H₂O by writing H₂ + O₂ → H₂O₂?
flashcards.back: H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide, a different substance. Changing a subscript changes the product.

questions.question: Which statement describes the law of conservation of mass?
options: Atoms are destroyed in reactions but new ones are made
The mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants
The products always have a greater mass than the reactants
Mass is only conserved in reactions that involve gases
markScheme: 1 mark: the mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants
questions.explanation: No atoms are lost or made, so total mass stays the same. Atoms are never destroyed or created in chemical reactions, and the law applies to every reaction.

questions.question: How many oxygen atoms are shown in 3CO₂?
questions.explanation: Each CO₂ contains 2 oxygen atoms and the coefficient 3 multiplies the whole formula: 3 × 2 = 6. Answers of 2 or 3 forget to multiply, and 5 adds instead of multiplying.

questions.question: Which of these equations is balanced?
questions.explanation: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO has 2 Mg and 2 O on each side. The other three each have 2 atoms of oxygen or chlorine on the left but only 1 on the right.

questions.question: What does the state symbol (aq) mean?
questions.explanation: (aq) stands for aqueous, a solution in water. A pure liquid such as water itself is (l), and a gas is (g).

questions.question:
Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid: Mg + __HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂
Which number is needed in front of HCl to balance the equation?
questions.explanation: The right-hand side has 2 chlorine atoms (in MgCl₂) and 2 hydrogen atoms (in H₂), so 2HCl is needed. 4 would give too many atoms of both.

questions.question: A student balances H₂ + O₂ → H₂O by writing H₂ + O₂ → H₂O₂. Why is this wrong?
options: There are now too many hydrogen atoms on the right
Changing the subscript changes the product to a different substance
Equations must always have a 2 in front of the first reactant
markScheme: 1 mark: changing the subscript changes the product to a different substance
questions.explanation: H₂O₂ is hydrogen peroxide, not water. Only coefficients may be changed. The correct equation is 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

questions.question: How many atoms in total are shown in Ca(OH)₂?
questions.explanation: Ca(OH)₂ contains 1 Ca, 2 O and 2 H atoms, total 5. Answering 3 or 4 forgets that the subscript 2 multiplies both atoms in the bracket.

A student puts copper sulfate solution and a small tube of sodium hydroxide solution into a flask. The student seals the flask with a bung and puts it on a balance.

The student tips the flask so that the solutions mix. A blue precipitate forms.
What happens to the reading on the balance?

It decreases because the solutions have been used up
questions.explanation: In a closed system nothing can enter or leave, and no atoms are lost or made, so the total mass does not change. A precipitate is made from atoms that were already in the solutions.

questions.question: Which equation for the reduction of iron(III) oxide by carbon monoxide is correctly balanced?
questions.explanation: Check oxygen: left 3 + 3 = 6, right 3 × 2 = 6. Iron 2 = 2 and carbon 3 = 3. The other options balance iron but not oxygen.

questions.question:
Magnesium reacts with oxygen to produce magnesium oxide.
12 g of magnesium reacts completely with 8 g of oxygen.
Calculate the mass of magnesium oxide produced.
questions.explanation: Mass of products = mass of reactants, so mass of magnesium oxide = 12 + 8 = 20 g.

questions.question:
A student heats calcium carbonate strongly. The calcium carbonate decomposes into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide gas.
Figure 1 shows the apparatus.
Table 1 shows the student's results. All the calcium carbonate decomposed.
Calculate the mass of carbon dioxide produced.

questions.explanation: Mass is conserved: the mass of calcium carbonate equals the total mass of the two products. 50 − 28 = 22 g of carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Calculate the total number of atoms in the formula 2H₂SO₄.
questions.explanation: One H₂SO₄ has 2 + 1 + 4 = 7 atoms. The coefficient 2 doubles this: 2 × 7 = 14.

questions.question:
Sodium reacts with chlorine to produce sodium chloride.
Table 1 shows the masses in one experiment. All of the sodium reacted.
Calculate the mass of chlorine that reacted.
questions.explanation: Mass of reactants = mass of products, so mass of chlorine = 11.7 − 4.6 = 7.1 g.

questions.question:
A student pours copper sulfate solution and sodium hydroxide solution into a beaker. A precipitate of copper hydroxide forms. No gas is produced.
Table 1 shows the masses of the solutions.
Calculate the total mass of the contents of the beaker after the reaction.
questions.explanation: No gas escapes, so all the products stay in the beaker and the mass is conserved: 52.4 + 48.6 = 101.0 g.

questions.question:
Ammonia is produced by the reaction:
N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃
Table 1 shows the masses in one reaction. All of the nitrogen reacted.
Calculate the mass of hydrogen that reacted.
questions.explanation: Mass is conserved, so the mass of hydrogen is 34 − 28 = 6 g. You do not need the coefficients for this calculation, only the total masses.

questions.question:
Aluminium burns in oxygen:
4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃
Table 1 shows the results of experiment 1. All of the aluminium reacted.
In experiment 2, a student uses twice the mass of aluminium and enough oxygen for all of it to react.
Calculate the mass of oxygen used in experiment 2.
markScheme: 1 mark: mass of oxygen in first experiment = 10.2 − 5.4 = 4.8 g
1 mark: masses are in the same ratio when the aluminium is doubled
questions.explanation: In the first experiment 4.8 g of oxygen reacts with 5.4 g of aluminium. Reactants always combine in a fixed ratio, so doubling the aluminium doubles the oxygen needed: 9.6 g.

questions.question: Explain why mass is conserved in a chemical reaction.
acceptedAnswers: no atoms are lost or made
atoms are not created or destroyed
same atoms in reactants and products
markScheme: 1 mark: no atoms are lost or made (created or destroyed)
1 mark: the atoms are just rearranged into new substances, so the total mass is the same
questions.explanation: The products contain exactly the same atoms as the reactants, joined in different ways. Since the atoms are the same, their total mass is the same.

questions.question:
Balance the equation for the reaction between hydrogen and chlorine.
H₂ + Cl₂ → HCl
questions.explanation: There are 2 H and 2 Cl on the left. Writing 2HCl gives 2 H and 2 Cl on the right.

questions.question:
Balance the equation for the reaction between lithium and oxygen.
Li + O₂ → Li₂O
questions.explanation: Oxygen: 2 on the left, so write 2Li₂O. This has 4 lithium atoms, so write 4Li. Check: Li 4 = 4, O 2 = 2.

questions.question:
Methane burns in oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and water.
CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O
Balance the equation and add state symbols. The water is produced as a gas.
questions.explanation: Balance hydrogen first (2H₂O gives 4 H), then oxygen: 2 + 2 = 4 oxygen atoms on the right, so 2O₂. Methane, oxygen, carbon dioxide and steam are all gases here.

questions.question:
Balance the equation for the reaction between zinc and hydrochloric acid.
Zn + HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂
questions.explanation: The products contain 2 H and 2 Cl, so 2HCl is needed. Zinc is already balanced.

questions.question:
Propane burns in oxygen.
Balance the equation for the complete combustion of propane.
C₃H₈ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O
questions.explanation: Carbon: 3 so 3CO₂. Hydrogen: 8 so 4H₂O. Oxygen on the right: 3 × 2 + 4 × 1 = 10, so 5O₂ on the left.

questions.question:
Aluminium displaces copper from copper sulfate solution.
Balance the equation for the reaction.
Al + CuSO₄ → Al₂(SO₄)₃ + Cu
questions.explanation: Treat SO₄ as a unit: there are 3 on the right, so 3CuSO₄, which needs 3Cu. Aluminium: 2 on the right, so 2Al.

questions.question:
Iron reacts with chlorine:
2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃
Show by counting atoms that the equation is balanced.
Give what the 3 in front of Cl₂ tells you.
markScheme: 1 mark: chlorine: 3 × 2 = 6 on the left and 2 × 3 = 6 on the right
1 mark: 3 molecules (units) of chlorine react for every 2 atoms of iron
questions.explanation: Counting each element on both sides proves the equation obeys conservation of mass. The coefficient shows the number of molecules of Cl₂ in the reaction ratio.

questions.question: State what is meant by a closed system.
acceptedAnswers: no substances can enter or leave
nothing can get in or out
markScheme: 1 mark: a system where no substances (matter) can enter or leave
questions.explanation: A sealed flask is a closed system. Because nothing can escape or enter, the mass of a closed system does not change during a reaction.

questions.question:
Aluminium reacts with oxygen to form aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃.
Write a balanced symbol equation for this reaction and explain each step you used to balance it.
markScheme: Indicative content: write correct formulae Al + O₂ → Al₂O₃; count atoms: left Al 1, O 2; right Al 2, O 3; oxygen: lowest common multiple of 2 and 3 is 6, so 3O₂ and 2Al₂O₃; this gives 4 Al on the right so 4Al on the left; check: Al 4 = 4, O 6 = 6; final 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃; only coefficients changed, not formulae.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct balanced equation with a clear, logical explanation including a final check.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): correct formulae with some attempt at balancing, or correct equation with no explanation.
questions.explanation: Oxygen is the awkward element because it appears as 2 atoms on one side and 3 on the other. Using 6 (the lowest common multiple) solves it, then aluminium follows: 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃.

questions.question: Describe an experiment to show that mass is conserved when solutions of copper sulfate and sodium hydroxide react to form a precipitate of copper hydroxide. Explain the results you would expect in terms of atoms.
markScheme: Indicative content: measure out the copper sulfate solution in one container and sodium hydroxide solution in another (for example a small test tube inside a conical flask); place everything on a balance and record the total mass; seal the flask with a bung so it is a closed system; tip or mix the solutions; blue precipitate forms; record the total mass again after the reaction; expected result: mass is the same before and after; explanation: no atoms are lost or made; atoms are rearranged to form copper hydroxide and sodium sulfate; no gas is made and nothing escapes; repeat to check results are repeatable; use a balance with a resolution of 0.01 g.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a clear, logical method using a closed system and weighing before and after, with the expected result fully explained in terms of atoms being rearranged and none being lost or made.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a workable method with weighing before and after, and some explanation of why the mass stays the same.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example weigh the chemicals and mix them, or mass stays the same, with little explanation.
questions.explanation: The key ideas are weighing the whole system (including containers) before and after mixing, keeping everything inside, and linking the unchanged mass to atoms being rearranged rather than lost or made.

questions.question:
Iron reacts with sulfur when heated to produce iron sulfide, FeS.
A student heats a mixture of iron and sulfur. After the reaction, some yellow sulfur is left over.
Table 1 shows the student's results.
Calculate the mass of sulfur left over.
Explain why some sulfur is left over.
markScheme: Indicative content: total mass of reactants = 5.6 + 4.0 = 9.6 g; mass of products = 8.8 g iron sulfide + leftover sulfur; leftover sulfur = 9.6 − 8.8 = 0.8 g; so 3.2 g of sulfur reacted; iron and sulfur combine in a fixed ratio; there was more sulfur than the iron could react with (sulfur in excess); total mass is still conserved.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct value of 0.8 g with clear working and an explanation that sulfur was in excess because elements combine in fixed proportions.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct working or a partial explanation.
questions.explanation: Mass is conserved across everything present at the end, including unreacted sulfur. 9.6 − 8.8 = 0.8 g of sulfur did not react because the 5.6 g of iron only needed 3.2 g of sulfur.
